title: Feeling Burned Out, Read This
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: A long essay on the inner work of teaching, in which Stuart starts from the aim of promoting students' long-term flourishing and lists four keys to an impactful career: knowing what you are after, internal work, taking care of business in the classroom, and working well with adults. He then concentrates on the 'You' level with four 'Jedi mind tricks': you are not your job, embrace failure as progress, aim for impact rather than popularity, and let teaching build your character. Each is grounded in personal story, including his dismal student-teaching term and his candid hallway conversation with a disengaged student called Belle. He argues that tying identity to performance ruins teachers through both success and failure, that failure is deliberate practice, and that seeking students' good rather than their approval ultimately wins their trust. The essay ends by inviting readers to add their own tricks for tending the heart and mind from which teaching flows.
points: Stuart argues burnout is avoided by cultivating a mind bent on impact and likens the heart and mind to a garden that needs constant tending and weeding.
He urges teachers to detach self-worth from job performance, because success inflates pride and jealousy while failure turns a bad day into a bad self.
His student-teaching story supplies the reframe that failure equals progress, since each failed experiment makes at least one person better: the teacher.
The Belle story shows that telling a student an honest, caring truth earned more trust than flattery would have, which is why he says to seek students' good, not their approval.
He closes with the claim that hardship can refine patience and self-control, so teachers can model the character strengths they want students to develop.
quotes: I've never met a teacher who didn't go into education hoping that they'd make a difference — that, ultimately, their work would promote the long-term flourishing of young people. There's no other way to begin talking about burnout than by starting with the ultimate aim of teaching: the long-term flourishing of our students.

So here's what few teacher books will tell you: great teaching is only possible when you are engaged with it with your mind and heart and soul, but this is hard because it's almost like present conditions were designed to rip out our hearts and drive us out of our minds and detach our souls. But our perception of present circumstances is malleable.

As a new teacher, I used to look down on older, burnt out teachers until I realized that none of them, years ago with newly minted teaching certificates in their hands, dreamed of one day becoming burnt out gripe-masters.

You will become proud; you will think you’re super amazing, God's gift to the profession. You will think you intrinsically merit greater attention than other teachers. You will expect to be honored frequently by the praise of others, and when others are praised instead of you, jealousy will sicken you like the stomach flu.

I went from the guy who fails mopingly to the guy who fails excitedly because of the lessons I was learning. It turned my worst days into some of my most productive; days in which my greatest weaknesses were laid bare like those nightmares where you realize you're not wearing any pants became days in which my strength as a teacher grew the most.

I didn't have time to think through all these things — she needed a response now. And this is why we have to cultivate our hearts — in moments like these, when there's no time for calculation, the basic orientation of our hearts comes forth from our lips; these tiny teacher decisions flow from who we are, so we have to do the work of making sure we are something worth flowing.
I'm not saying be a jerk to kids — I am saying you've got to have higher goals than to simply have them love you. Them loving you makes you popular, but not necessarily a good teacher.
